sections.title: 5. Two Ways to Solve a DP Problem
5. How to Approach Any 1D DP Problem

blocks.text: Before patterns and problems, let's understand what dynamic programming actually is and why it exists.
Let's start with a simple example. Calculate the 5th Fibonacci number.
fib(5) = fib(4) + fib(3)
Simple enough. But look at what happens when you expand it fully:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406196577-730294666.png
Notice something? fib(3) is calculated twice. fib(2) is calculated three times. The same subproblems keep getting solved over and over again.
For fib(5) it doesn't matter much. But for fib(50)?

items: Without DP, recursion repeats the same calculations again and again, leading to exponential calls (billions for fib(50)).
With DP, each value is computed only once and reused, so only 50 calculations are needed.

blocks.text: This reduces time from exponential to linear.
That is the problem dynamic programming solves stop recalculating what you already know.
Dynamic programming is a technique where you:

items: Break the problem into smaller similar subproblems so it becomes easier to solve step by step.
Ensure each subproblem is solved only once to avoid repeated work.
Store the result of each solved subproblem in memory.
Reuse the stored results whenever the same subproblem appears again.

blocks.text: The storing part is called memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up). More on that shortly.
Not every problem can be solved with DP. Two conditions must be true:
Condition 1: Overlapping Subproblems
The same smaller problems appear again and again.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406196577-427572189.png
fib(5) needs fib(3), and fib(4) also needs fib(3), so fib(3) is computed multiple times.
Similarly, fib(3) needs fib(1), and fib(2) also needs fib(1), so fib(1) is repeated.
This shows overlapping subproblems, where the same values are recalculated again and again in recursion.e
Dynamic Programming avoids this by computing each value once and reusing it.
If every subproblem is unique and never repeats DP adds no value.
Condition 2: Optimal Substructure
The solution to the big problem is built from solutions to smaller problems.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406196577-461411790.png

fib(5) is built using results of smaller subproblems, fib(4) and fib(3).
Each of those is itself a smaller version of the same problem.
This shows optimal substructure, where the solution to a bigger problem depends on solutions to smaller problems of the same type.
If you cannot build the final answer from subproblem answers — DP won't work.
In 1D DP, you store your results in a single array one dimension.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406196578-111939672.png
Each index represents the answer to a subproblem. To solvedp[i], you look back at previous values in the same array.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197057-688970072.png
This is the simplest form of DP and the foundation for everything harder.

content.title: 5. Two Ways to Solve a DP Problem

blocks.text: Approach 1: Top Down (Memoization)
Start from the big problem. Break it down recursively. Store results as you go so you never solve the same thing twice.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197057-704274308.png
You start from the main problem, like fib(5), and break it down into smaller problems using recursion.
While going down, whenever you compute a value (like fib(2) or fib(3)), you store it.
If the same subproblem appears again, you don’t recompute it, you directly return the stored value.
This avoids repeated work and makes the solution efficient.
Think of it as solving the big problem by breaking it into smaller ones, and while returning back from recursion, you store each computed result so it can be reused later.
Approach 2: Bottom Up (Tabulation)
Start from the smallest subproblems and solve them first, then use those results to build up to bigger problems step by step.
You fill values in order (like fib(0), fib(1), fib(2), …) until you reach the final answer.
No recursion is used, and each value is computed only once using previously stored results.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197058-301805888.png

items: Start by initializing base cases, dp[0] = 0 and dp[1] = 1.
Then compute dp[2] using dp[1] and dp[0], which gives 1.
Next compute dp[3] using dp[2] and dp[1], which gives 2.
Then compute dp[4] using dp[3] and dp[2], which gives 3.
Finally compute dp[5] using dp[4] and dp[3], which gives 5.

blocks.text: Think of it as starting from the smallest known values, then combining them step by step to build larger results until you reach the final answer.

blocks.text: Both approaches give the same result, but bottom-up is usually preferred because it avoids recursion and uses less overhead.
Space Optimization
In many 1D DP problems, the current value depends only on the last one or two values. So instead of storing the entire dp array, you can just keep track of those few previous values.
For Fibonacci, each value depends only on the previous two, so you only need two variables instead of an array.
Fibonacci:  dp[i] only needs dp[i-1] and dp[i-2]
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406197058-424992035.png
Instead of storing the entire DP array, you only keep the last two values.
Start with prev2 = 0 and prev1 = 1.
At each step, compute the current value as curr = prev1 + prev2.
Then shift the values forward by setting prev2 = prev1 and prev1 = curr.
Repeat this until you reach the required position, and prev1 will hold the final answer.
By keeping only the last two values instead of the full array, space usage reduces from O(n) to O(1), while still producing the same result.

content.title: 5. How to Approach Any 1D DP Problem

blocks.text:
Step 1: Define the state clearly
Decide what dp[i] represents, like “answer up to index i” or “ways to reach i”.

Step 2: Find the relation (transition)
Figure out how to compute dp[i] using previous values.

Step 3: Set base cases
Initialize the smallest values that can be solved directly.

Step 4: Build from small to large
Fill the dp array step by step so that previous results are already available.

Step 5: Extract the final answer
Return the required result, usually dp[n] or dp[n-1].
